utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we continue with the examination of the witness, Mr. Lukic, when I -- apparently there may be a problem with the audio for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it okay now, Mr. Mladic? It's okay now? Thank you, Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, yesterday when I said that it was not always clear to the Chamber what was in dispute and what the line of the cross-examination was, you more or less offered to briefly explain when I said that it should not be done in the presence of the witness. If you think it would assist the Chamber to briefly explain, I'm thinking in terms of not more than one, two, or two and a half minutes, then I certainly would give you an opportunity to do so. So I leave it to you. If you think it would help, please proceed; if not, we'll ask the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What our goal through this cross-examination is, is actually that we try to show that since there are -- is no bodies, there is no evidence, that these murders didn't happen, that this witness wasn't at the spot at the time, and that if anything happened could only happen by locals, civilians, and so on. That's the line of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- questions we are heading to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so there's a -- the position of the Defence is that the number of people as found in the annex to the indictment were not killed there?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since we got this list yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- we'll have to elaborate a bit on it because we -- as much as we were able to investigate since yesterday, I will show him three death certificates from the list, actually from the people he listed yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear now what the line of the Defence is in this respect and this might better enable the Chamber to understand your line of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One more thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- if I may. Regarding the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted to address that, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I want to address is the following: The Prosecution asked for two hours; they used effectively two hours and 14 minutes. You indicated in the beginning that you'd like to use 60 per cent, which would be 80 minutes. You used a little bit over 40 minutes to that. But until now - but that might change today - the Chamber, in view of the questions you've put to the witness, we've thought that 80 minutes would be a reasonable time. If you, however, have done additional research for those persons which I then may take it were not mentioned in any earlier statements? Does this come as a new element? The Chamber of course doesn't read all statements if it's -- if the witness is presented viva voce. But if the names of victims are entirely new, then of course that may change the situation. Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, some of the names may have been new. I believe there are a couple of them and I'd have to go back and double-check --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: -- that were mentioned in previous testimony and statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Some of them appeared in earlier statements. That's what you say, Mr. Lukic. You would agree with that, that some do and some do not appear in previous statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I can recall right now is that he did mention those names but as persons who left Vecici but not as killed persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think the question yesterday whether it was in the tunnel or after the tunnel that he had seen them last, that was what the question was about. Thank you for your explanation. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, the Chamber has considered whether we would hear your response to the four urgent motions immediately at the start of today's hearing or after we will have heard the evidence of Mr. Pasic. The Chamber preferred to see whether we could first conclude the testimony of Mr. Pasic and then hear your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Lukic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, good day, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day. [In English] Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now you were leaving Garici and going to Bilice. Your brother is already in Bilice; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't hear in my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Channel 4. English or would you like to hear the questions in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then channel 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, he'll follow in English, it's easier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you put your next question --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then we'll see whether the witness is at ease with what he hears.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pasic, now you were leaving Garici and going to Bilice. Your brother at that moment when you arrive in Bilice is already there; right?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And he said that Bilice would not hold out for long. How many people took part in the fighting in Bilice? I don't know what the right pronunciation is, Bilica or Bilice?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea how many soldiers were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know how many wounded or dead there were in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. You've been telling us about all this time I went from this place to that place, so you were moving about freely, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can say yes, but we were actually travelling most of the time and most of our travel we would go at night to avoid any -- to avoid any contact with the Serbs or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you cross any lines of fire? You say that you went to Bilice, that you went to Vecici. How did you manage to do that if there is fighting underway?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we went from Garici to Vecici, that was arranged by the truce signed five days between people from Vecici and the Serbs. So we were allowed to walk with no ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know about these people in Vecici, who they belonged to from a military point of view?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people in Vecici, I would assume they were local ones trying to defend themselves from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that they belonged to the Territorial Defence of Kotor Varos --

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if they -- if there was an army or any -- anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't remember. All right. After this you went to Garici yet again. You say that some people stayed in Bilice. These people in Bilice, they surrendered to the Serb forces and they safely went to Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. After my brother informed us that he learned that they're going to surrender, my mom was afraid that they heard from previous convoys and people leaving Kotor Varos that they were taking kids and the males away from the mother. And that's when he offered us to go back to Garici. But we would find out later that most of them who were at Bilice and surrendered did indeed survive. A lot of males were actually stripped-down at Brdo Vlasici and they were beaten, but most of them -- I think everyone did survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about whether you knew about the ultimatum, or rather, whether an ultimatum had ever been issued. Do you know that the Red Cross, the International Red Cross, also came to Vecici during the cease-fire? Were you there? Did you see these people from the Red Cross? Did you see them coming there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't see them?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anybody from Red Cross during my time in Vecici.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did not attend meetings of military leaders from Vecici with the people who came to negotiate; right?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I was just with my father. I missed him so much for the time that we got separated, so no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we may conclude that even if there had been some negotiations or preconditions or ultimatums, you wouldn't have known about any of that?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned before, I know the one that we were -- when we were in the Garici, according to my cousin Akif Pasic, when he told us that they did indeed sign the truce with the Serbs, that's the one that I know because we were sitting in the same room. As far as the other ones during my time in Vecici, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in Vecici there were about 1.000 armed men?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: People who left Vecici with you were armed; right? They did not leave their weapons behind in Vecici, they did not set out unarmed?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we left Vecici, I would say that their -- the long group that I joined also had a lot of people that were just walking, male. I've seen some weapons, yes, but not all the group had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the fighting in Vecici and around Vecici took place from May until November 1992?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As a matter of fact, I experienced most of them by going from place to place, and especially when we were in Cirkino Brdo I was a witness of air-strikes at Vecici; I've seen that. When we were in Garici, we've seen a fight between Vecici and the Serb forces, yes. And during my time in Bilice, that part of Bilice was also -- had a fight with the Serbs on the Kotor Varos line. Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who supplied weapons and uniforms to the people in Vecici? You say that your brother worked on supplies?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that my brother was -- I said that my brother's job, task, was to take the food and the water to the line, front line. As far as who supplied, as we all know, Vecici and Kotor Varos was surrounded by Serbs, so I don't think we -- I don't know, as a matter of fact, that they had any weapons or supplies going in and out of Vecici. I just know that my brother, his task, he was young and he was just supplying that and people in the front line with the water and the food.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Did you hear about the number of casualties there, how many people were killed or injured by the shelling? You spent two days in Vecici before you left; right?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. I know I learned from the people when I was in school Grabovica that -- when one of the guards asked us that they found out that air-strikes was on Vecici, how many people -- they wanted to know how many people died from air-strikes and the people who lived at that time in Vecici says that approximately hundred people died. I don't have -- during my time in Vecici, I know that there was a truce and except that second night the shelling started, I don't know how many people indeed died. But as far as the total from the time, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude that people from Vecici decided not to surrender to the Serb forces; rather, to fight their way out of the encirclement; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could we split up composite questions. Not to surrender is one and to fight is another. Could you please split up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As His Honour, Judge Orie, said, I am going to put two questions to you now. Were the people in Vecici surrounded by the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they decide to fight their way out of this encirclement instead of surrender?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilians decided to surrender. Males, including a lot -- I would say 500 to 700, approximately, the line decided to go to the safe passage, to Travnik, because we were afraid that they were -- be detained and taken in Banja Luka and Skender Vakuf, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So the people who were not civilians and you four boys were with them and three women, the remaining 500 to 700 persons started their breakthrough?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said ten women, five to six boys, yes, and all -- most of the men did indeed -- we started walking towards the safe passage, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, can we change it to English, please. I'm getting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Mr. Lukic, meanwhile I observed that through the back door you did the same, that is to combine -- you put formally two questions but the second question was exactly the same composite question as the first one. That is, you give the witness: Either surrender or fight your way out. There are other options like trying to escape unseen. I mean, could you please refrain from this kind of implicit suggestions which may not be noticed by the witness. And could you also consider that if I make such comment, that not through the back door you do exactly the same as I invited you not to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you told us about your journey, you were ambushed. You had two casualties. Then you split up. Then you met up with this other group. Yet then again you're surrounded. How many people were killed then when you were surrounded the second time?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am so sorry, sir, can you repeat the question. I'm getting ... I'm sorry, can you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Sure. [Interpretation] How many people lost their lives -- actually, first you were ambushed. Then you said that two persons lost their lives then. Then you split up. Then you met up with this other group, as you had reunited; you get some rest. Yet again, you are surrounded and then you are in cross-fire. You told us of how the bullets reminded you of insects. Do you know how many people lost their lives then?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned on the first ambush, Zec and his two sons, so three; and then on the second ambush, I witnessed Besim, his legs blown away on the mines. Approximately ten people in that -- when we got to that level area on that -- on the hill, there were people down there, approximately ten were injured -- and I don't know, I think we learned later that Besim indeed killed himself because he was asking somebody to finish him. And I don't know, but a total of ten people were in that river from the mines. I don't know what happened on the other side and how many casualties were on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Then ten people came across land-mines and got killed, and you say that out of this group of yours about 200 people crossed the river and joined up with you. And then you prayed with the imam on the other side of the river. Where are the others out of the 700? We heard about 25 casualties or so, the ones that you witnessed.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know on side in the tunnel we counted 200, approximately 200, anywhere from 150 to 200. I don't know what happened except when we were praying I remember the other side that people -- I assume they were the people who stood up to Serbs and decided to fight. At one point they were waving at us. I assumed they belonged to the long group. I don't know how many people were there or anything, but I know they were waving at us and I wish that we went that way instead of going to the tunnel and surrendering. Maybe we had a chance to survive then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you spoke about this group that took you from the tunnel towards Grabovica, and you also talk about a woman soldier. The woman was in uniform; right?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a Serb, camouflage uniform, a woman. She had a weapon, yes, not with -- in our group. I didn't -- nobody as far as the women had any weapon, but it was on the Serb side when we got out, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That group that took you to Grabovica, to the school, what did they look like? Did they have different uniforms or the same uniforms? Were they armed, some of them or all of them? What did they wear on their heads? Can you tell us a bit more about that?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. When we got to the courtyard of -- because when we were walking down we were instructed not to look around or anything, but I remember when we were in the courtyard and we were looking at the soldier across, they were lined up, I noticed they were all in camouflage uniform and I noticed that some of them they had -- the flag on the left -- left arm. I noticed the soldiers had the flag with the stripes. They were all in camouflage uniform. I didn't see the hats except the generals I'm notice -- the general, he had some pins on his shoulder. They were not masked whatsoever. They didn't have anything over their head. They were just -- seemed like more organised army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. And then you were addressed by the man who was wearing a hat, the kind of hat miners wear, with a lamp on it. He told you that your men would pay. For what were the men supposed to pay? Did he elaborate?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I remember is just he told us that we are going to spend the night in the school, and the next morning we are going to go for Travnik and nothing's going to happen to us but your men will pay for this. I don't know what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to know when you were at the school. Reading various statements, I did not quite understand this. Did your mother go upstairs to see your father?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mom was not with me. I don't know where this came from. My mom was left in Vecici and they were all civilians. We joined them when we came with the buses. She was not with me in the school, in the classroom --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's enough. Thank you. But you said in your statement this man told you that the fighters would pay. You didn't say "men" but "fighters." But never mind, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, whenever you refer to a statement, the Chamber would like to know what statement you're referring to, because as I said before this is a viva voce witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I think that we clarified that there were fighters, so we don't have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but if you refer to a statement we'd like to know what you're referring to. That's the only thing I'm bringing to your attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next morning in Grabovica you were at the school. You leave the school and there were civilians waiting there, mainly women and children; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And some elderly people, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Women, children, and the elderly. They attack you; right? That is the gauntlet you have to go through, right, the gauntlet of elderly men, women and children?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, from the school to the bus, yes, the horrible thing. Physically we were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And a woman wearing black grabbed you and tried to kill you with her knife; right? At that moment you were saved by a soldier who grabbed you away from that woman and threw you onto the bus. Did you say this soldier saved your life?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that he saved my life by throwing me in the bus, yes. I don't know if I would live, I have no idea, but he indeed grabbed me and threw me in the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that, you don't know what happened later in Grabovica. After you left, after you spent those 15 minutes on the bus you left and you don't know what happened afterwards in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened, but there's no doubt in my mind - and after I learned that they found the remainings of my uncle - they were all killed, my dad and everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm just asking. You don't know, you don't have first-hand knowledge what happened there? Speaking of that, yesterday you mentioned Nedzad Menzil.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I call up in e-court 65 ter 6661.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have the document in English in front of you; right?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't need Serbian version since this gentleman is reading English, so if you can only put the English version, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, I'll tell you which line -- fifth line from the top below the subheading "statement of reasons." Fifth line reads: [In English] "The applicant -- the applicant, Muharem Menzil submitted an application to this court seeking to establish the death of his son, Nedzad Menzil." And then it says: "'My son was killed by Serbian Chetnik extremists in a place called Duboko, in the municipality of Kotor Varos on 3 November 1992.'" [Interpretation] Do you know that Nedzad Menzil in fact lost his life in a place called Duboko, not in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I know his father was there and this Nedzad was my age. I don't know if we are talking about the same, but he was shot in the stomach and -- yeah, I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. The next document I'd like to call up --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I would like to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 6661 will become Exhibit D1, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] The next document is 6665, 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here Munira Opakic from Hrvacani seeks that her son, Sevad Opakic be declared dead, and in line 3 she says: [In English] "Her son was a member of TO Kotor Varos and that he disappeared on 3 November 1992, together with a large group of people ..." This "people" is a wrong translation since in the original document it says "combatants." So I would like to have this document corrected in this way. People in the booths can check Serbian version if they want and see that it says "saboraca," [Interpretation] "co-fighters," [In English] not people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- in the next break could specifically this word be verified - apart from that of course a correction of an official translation should be done by CLSS - but to see whether the parties could already agree on whether there may be a mistake in translation. Another option would be to invite the witness to read the relevant portion in B/C/S, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, can you still read B/C/S? If we were to put the B/C/S version on the screen.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have B/C/S version on the e-court. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, in the middle we see "obrazlozenje," statement of reasons. Start with line 3, "in her application ..." and read that sentence up to the words "without a trace ..."

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to read this or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, please. From the third line starting with "u svom prijedlogu ...," [Interpretation] "in her application."

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In her application, the applicant states that her son was a member of the TO Kotor Varos and that during an attempted breakthrough on the 3rd of November, 1992, in the area of Grabovica together with a large group of co-fighters he was ambushed by the Chetniks and has not been seen since."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you say: I saw ten people get killed in the ambush. You didn't see what happened on the other side. Do you allow for the possibility that this man got killed during the ambush, that he found himself in together with his co-fighters?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Absolutely not because right before we got to the tunnel he was in the same group because I can hear him, he was right next to me because of his injuries being in Vecici from the shell because he was making a weird noise. And he was there in the tunnel and we all went down to Grabovica. He was there with me. I can see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You think that Munira Opakic, his mother, gave wrong information to the municipal court in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, would you please clarify this matter in an appropriate way. The mother apparently was not present, was she, so the first question - and that is of course true for this document and for the other document as well - is what the source of knowledge is. And then to ask whether someone is not telling the truth would require at least to pay attention to whether that person had received information from others or whether she personally observed what had happened, because telling the truth depends on what your knowledge is when you give a statement. Would you please clarify all that instead of implicit suggesting that this person would have personally observed what happened and by giving this statement was telling the truth what she observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't say, Your Honour, that she didn't tell the truth, but she gave the wrong information to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but there's a suggestion in it, isn't it? What's the wrong information; what's the right information? The information she gave is the information she may have had from whatever source. And then to ask this witness -- that doesn't make sense, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For me it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and keep in mind my observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll finish with the looting at Vlasic. You say at a distance of 15 metres there were four groups of those men who were jumping out and coming in. Did you get off the bus or did the men at Vlasic get on to the bus, the men who robbed you; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember clearly. When we were parked, all the buses were parked and they were letting a few buses at a time, the civilians, to go to this path and I can see clearly. They wouldn't let us at the same time. They would let two or three buses and then they would stop. We would go -- we were at the last bus that joined the group, so we never came back to the bus again. We were just told to go, walk slowly, and as we were walking, these people -- the soldiers were jumping and they had their faces covered and they were asking for gold, money, every so many metres down I think three or four times we were -- different groups would -- until we finally reached the Bosnian side we were jumped by these people and asked for the money and the valuables.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How far was one group of them from another? What distance did you go from one group of them to the other?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember approximately, but I know I just -- as soon as I -- we got stripped down, I was running trying to catch my mom because she was in front of me. I was passing people that actually were released before me so I was just trying to get to my mom. I don't know the distance I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll put it differently. Could one group see the other? Were they close together?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were able to catch up to the other group to -- some people were not able to walk, the civilians. I don't know as far as the soldiers, I don't know how far they were apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry. [Interpretation] Those who were robbing you, were they able to see one another? Was one group of them able to see the other group?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was so scared. I have no idea if they were able to see each other. I don't know. My goal was to find my mom. That's what I was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say the first time everything was taken from you, not a needle was left on you, and that happened by the tunnel. Then the first group takes everything. Then you go on. Then you are robbed again by the next group at Vlasic, although you had been robbed twice already. That's what I can't understand. What was the fourth group in a row at Vlasic able to steal from you? Were you able to hide something the first, second, and third time from those people who were robbing you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We need to state here that we joined the buses, the civilians, from Vecici. Our bus, we didn't have anything. We were stripped down in Grabovica. So I know these people jumped in front of us. They were constantly asking for money. And as a matter of fact, I remember one had a knife and asked me, Do you have money? And I said, No, I don't have anything. I remember that soldier. And every group who stopped the people and they were separating people and going through their belongings. That's why I say there was a period when I was literally walking on top of the clothes and these belongings because they were opening everything and looking for the money and belongings. And every group was doing the same thing. We -- I didn't have anything and I don't know if the people -- the rest of the buses had something that they were interested in, but obviously the purpose was trying to get as much as they were able to get. I didn't have anything. I was not able to give anything anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 6665 would become Exhibit D2, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: First, Mr. Pasic, I would like to ask just a couple of follow-up questions that arose with respect to questions that arose on cross-examination yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was at page 605, lines roughly 4 through 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You were asked about the difference in the status of villages that -- of people from Muslim villages based upon whether the village was resisting or fighting versus those who were not. Do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you know whether the village of Dabovci signed a loyalty oath?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, because I'll tell you -- because I had to -- at one point when we were in Garici, I decided to go with my mom because we knew about our sister. We went to -- and see her. We travelled from Garici to Dabovci to see her. And at that moment they were -- we were glad to see her because we were worrying about each other. And they had signed -- indeed they signed the loyalty to the Serbs, that Dabovci did, as well as Cirkino Brdo, Hanifici, Garici, Vakufci.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And with respect to the people from Dabovci, do you know whether they were safe and lived throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. They were -- after they signed the truce or the loyalty to the Serbs, we learned horrible thing happened. My sister, her husband, a lot of men from Dabovci, all the men --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, but I have to object at this point. This is something that goes beyond the direct examination. It doesn't come from my cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, yesterday - and I believe at the lines -- page and lines that I referred to - the witness was asked with respect to whether his village was treated differently because they did not sign a loyalty oath and there were questions about the safety of various villages that did sign a loyalty oath. I believe this is appropriate cross-examination -- or, excuse me, re-direct from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We've -- when we were in Garici, we've noticed that Dabovci, the houses were on fire and then people were taken from Dabovci, some to Vrbanjci and well-known place Kozara. And when we got to Vecici, also we learned from talking to Lihovic Elvir who is the only one who survived, and we heard the stories but we wanted to hear -- and I was in the room with my mom when she asked him, How did he survive? What happened there? And he says that the soldiers when they came in, in the village, they were mad and ordered all the men to get out and grouped them all together and put them in a barn, including his cousin, a close friend across. They were all put in this barn and the Serb soldiers fired the weapons and his friend grabbed them, went over hand and after they were down, the bullets didn't go through him. They burned, they threw some hand-grenades in there. He broke through the window and escaped across to the river. And rest of the civilians were taken, including my sister. He says that if it wasn't up to his friend that -- he is the only one who survived from there, because he saved them, he held them close and the bullets didn't go through him and the hand-grenade and the fire. He managed to break the window and crawl out this barn and cross the river, and he's the only one who survived and then he ended up with us at Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: When is the last time that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him in the tunnel and going down this field, he was close to us because we tried to stay together. He was down there with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Finally, when you were in the classroom at the school in Grabovica, you saw the military trucks and the men and the lights, were any of those men fighting or resisting?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Their hands were tied behind their back. I remember clearly seeing that night. It was raining hard. Their hands were tied behind their back and they were brought on the second floor. They did not fight. They were tied, their hands were tied. They didn't have no weapons, nothing. They were just walking with their heads down.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And have you or, to the best of your knowledge, anyone else found your father's remains?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, since I'm re-living and going back to this, I had a dream about my dad last night. For the first time I was able to see his face. I'm glad because most of the dreams, nightmares that I have from personal experience, I was always trying to reach him. I saw his face last night. I find out, I don't remember, I think it was in 2007 I don't -- I'm not sure that the remaining of my uncle they found part of his finger in Plitska. I miss my dad even more so now with being a father and having my own kids. Everything I do with them brings the memories back. And I urge people that listen to this and watch this, if they have any information please come forward and let us find -- let me find my dad, please. I'd like to find my dad and my cousins. Come forward, please. I miss my dad.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions from the Prosecution. Mr. Lukic, has the re-examination of the witness triggered any questions in rejoinder?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to -- Mr. Lukic, if you wish to tender that from the bar table, the Chamber would not oppose that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we give the Prosecution an opportunity to call its next witness, I would like to deal with a few procedural matters, the first one being that the Chamber would like to give an oral decision. It is a decision on the Prosecution's submission on amendment to its witness list in light of the Trial Chamber's decision on adjudicated facts. On the 2nd of May, 2012, the Chamber issued its fourth decision on adjudicated facts concerning the rebuttal evidence procedure. In that decision, the Chamber instructed the Prosecution to file a notification within one week, indicating the number of hours which will not be used and the number and identities of witnesses who will not be called in light of the Chamber's decision on adjudicated facts. The Chamber purposefully chose a one-week dead-line in light of the fact that the instruction at issue had originally been issued in the Chamber's first decision on adjudicated facts, which was filed on the 28th of February of this year. On the 13th of March, 2012, the Prosecution had requested that the original dead-line for this notification be postponed until after the Chamber's fourth decision was issued. On the 29th of March of this same year at a Status Conference, the Chamber granted the Prosecution request. However, the Chamber also made clear that the dead-line would be no more than one week from the filing of the fourth decision and further stressed, and I quote, "that the Prosecution should already be preparing now instead of beginning to work on this after the filing of the decision." I refer the parties in this respect to transcript page 268. As previously stated, the fourth decision was filed on the 2nd of May, 2012. On the 9th of May, the Prosecution filed its submission in which it argues that it would be premature for it to make any decisions on withdrawal of witnesses until the Defence requests for certification to appeal the Chamber's first, second, and third decisions on adjudicated facts is either denied or the relevant appellate proceedings concluded. Once either of these occurs and the matter of the Chamber's judicial notice of adjudicated facts is finalised, the Prosecution submits that it will need another seven weeks to conduct a review before making amendments to its Rule 65 ter witness list. On the 27th of June, 2012, the Chamber granted certification to appeal its first, second, and third decisions on adjudicated facts. In relation to the Prosecution s submission, the Chamber first clarifies that it did not instruct the Prosecution to amend its Rule 65 ter witness list. The Chamber does not expect witnesses to be removed from the witness list or placed on a "reserve witness list," as proposed by the Prosecution in its submission. For clarity, the Chamber's instruction is for the Prosecution, and I quote, "to file a notification indicating the number of hours which will not be used, and the number and identity of witnesses who will not be called in light of the Chamber taking judicial notice of the proposed facts listed in the first, second, and third decisions." The Chamber also takes this opportunity to explain the rationale for this instruction. The purpose was to ensure that the Prosecution, as the party who requested that adjudicated facts be judicially noticed by this Chamber, was actively reviewing and reducing - when appropriate - the evidence it plans to adduce in this case in light of judicial notice having been taken of facts upon which the Prosecution would otherwise have presented evidence. One of the primary rationales of Rule 94 of the Rules is judicial economy, and one of the legal effects of a Chamber judicially noticing facts adjudicated by another Trial Chamber is that it relieves the proposing party of its initial burden of production on those facts. In sum, taking judicial notice of adjudicated facts avoids the duplicative presentation of evidence in relation to those same facts, unless they are put back into question by the other party through the introduction of contradictory evidence. In relation to the fact that the Chamber has granted certification to appeal its decisions on adjudicated facts, the Chamber stresses that it fully expects the Prosecution to not present evidence that overlaps with judicially noticed adjudicated facts during the period before an Appeals Chamber decision is issued. This should be clear from the instruction which I read out yesterday in the amendment and clarification of the guidance on the presentation and tendering of evidence, and I will repeat part of it now. I quote: "For each viva voce witness and for each Rule 92 bis, ter, quater, and Rule 94 bis motion, the Chamber expects the parties to carefully review which portions of the anticipated evidence relate to adjudicated facts and which may, therefore, no longer be necessary and to reduce its evidence accordingly." This is the end of this quote. The Chamber therefore decides that for all witnesses who appear during the interim period before any Appeals Chamber decision is issued, the Prosecution should review on a witness-by-witness basis the evidence it intends to adduce in accordance with the instruction contained in the guidance just mentioned. Once an Appeals Chamber decision is issued, the Prosecution is instructed to file a notification within seven weeks of the decision, indicating for all remaining witnesses listed on its witness list the number of hours which will not be used and the number and identities of witnesses who will not be called in light of the Chamber's decisions on adjudicated facts. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. Mr. Groome, the Chamber would like to hear the response by the Prosecution on the four Defence motions which were filed yesterday; that is, request for adjournment, request to postpone the cross-examination of the evidence of Mr. Dannatt, barring one Harland document, and barring 26 other Harland documents. These are summarised, the four requests that were made in motions yesterday. You have an opportunity to orally respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Does the Chamber have any preference for the order in which I take each of these motions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As long as it is clear to us, but perhaps postponing the Dannatt cross to be first, adjournment motion second, barring one document mentioned by Harland third, and barring 26 documents mentioned by Harland fourth would have our preference. But as long as it's clear to us what you are dealing with, we have no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. So I'll deal with the application to adjourn the cross-examination of General Dannatt first. Is that the -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, let me just check the record. Yes, that's the first one you asked me to deal with. He is the Prosecution military expert who is scheduled to testify this week. The Prosecution reiterates that it will not oppose a reasonable Defence request to re-call General Dannatt for further cross-examination, a possibility the Chamber also recognised in paragraph 18 of its 5th of July decision on the presentation of the first segment of the Prosecution case. In this respect we believe the Defence is in error in paragraph 13 of its motion insofar as it suggests that the Chamber has precluded it from re-calling General Dannatt for cross-examination. The Chamber's decision regarding General Dannatt does not address the possibility of re-calling the witness -- I'm sorry, does not address the possibility of re-calling the witness, which the Defence should seek upon identifying sufficient cause -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. The Chamber has opened this possibility for the Defence. In our view -- our view is that the possibility of re-calling General Dannatt for additional cross-examination, if justified, is sufficient to protect the accused's rights. However, regarding the Defence's ability to prepare to cross-examine General Dannatt at this time, I will respond to the three claims made in this motion as well as in the Defence motion regarding General Dannatt filed on the 2nd of July. The Defence asserts that it has had insufficient time to prepare to cross-examine General Dannatt because, one, it received General Dannatt's curriculum vitae recently, particularly in the Serbian language; two, General Dannatt is now the third witness in the Prosecution case, while he was initially scheduled as the 23rd witness to testify; and three, the Defence received certain materials regarding General Dannatt this past week. These arguments are misleading. First, General Dannatt's curriculum vitae is set out at some length in his current report as well as in his previous report drafted for the Krstic case, to which the Defence has had access since November 2011 in both the original English and the B/C/S translation. The Defence has had more than sufficient opportunity to review his professional background and one member of the current Mladic Defence is the very counsel that cross-examined General Dannatt in the Krstic case, and, as I understand it, will be cross-examining him in this case. Second, as the Trial Chamber noted in its 5th of July decision regarding the scheduling of the first segment, the projected date for General Dannatt's testimony has not changed since the 13th of April. Defence has had clear and consistent notice as to when General Dannatt would be testifying. The only difference is that fewer other witnesses are testifying before he takes the stand. Finally, the Defence did receive certain materials this past week. General Dannatt's report refers to critical materials in the body of the report by their ERN's and/or their 65 ter numbers. It also notes in paragraph 4 that General Dannatt reviewed other materials in the course of preparing his report, materials he did not cite for conclusions drawn in the report. I would note for Your Honours in this regard the decision in the Stanisic and Simatovic case of the 11th of March, 2011, holding that Chambers evaluate the disclosure of materials related to an expert's report on a case-by-case basis and the decision in the Gotovina et al. case of 27 August 2009, holding that there is no obligation for the Defence to disclose to the Prosecution materials and communications pertaining to the preparation or production of an expert report or the expert's testimony. The Defence did not request any of the materials now at issue until approximately two weeks ago, at which time we agreed with the Defence that we would provide them with a copy of the Prosecution binder that we had prepared for our team, which included all of the exhibits cited in his report. Those materials had been disclosed to the Defence in the context of the overall disclosure in this case. We also agreed to provide an index of materials that were provided generally to General Dannatt but which he did not rely upon in his report. The Defence agreed to that proposal and we provided the binder and the index shortly after. The Defence now complains that the index includes non-ERN'd material. That material consists in its entirety of a previous version of the indictment in this trial and three lists of personalities in the VRS. This information is all publicly available and is not at issue in the case. Your Honours, the Prosecution provided materials related to the production of General Dannatt's report to the Defence upon and shortly following the Defence request to facilitate Defence preparations in accord with our own obligation to ensure fairness of the proceedings. We will maintain our commitment not to oppose reasonable requests to re-call General Dannatt for further cross-examination, but in our view is that the Defence has had sufficient time to prepare to begin its cross-examination at the conclusion of General Dannatt's testimony in chief, and it should be called upon to do that at that time. Your Honour, my response to the request for an adjournment based on a change in the guide-lines. The Defence yesterday filed a motion seeking a six-month continuance of the proceedings on the basis of the Trial Chamber's decision, modifying its guidance regarding Rule 92 bis, Rule 92 ter, and Rule 92 quater. In that respect -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. This motion was filed at the 11th hour of trial preparations. It asserts the recent modification in the Chamber's guidance creates significant impediments in Defence preparations and violates the accused's fair trial rights. The Defence has not previously made this argument, even though the Chamber's guide-lines have been under reconsideration for several months since most recently the Prosecution's oral submissions on the 3rd of May, 2012. The Defence has never asserted that the guide-lines impacted their fair trial rights and should be estopped from making such a pretextual argument at this juncture. Moreover, previous Defence filings regarding the guide-lines have not characterised them as absolute rules upon which the Defence was relying in its preparations for trial, as this motion does. Paragraph 4 of the Defence 16th of April, 2012, filing regarding the guide-line says, instead: "They are exactly as they are termed, guide-lines." The Chamber has repeated stated that variation is allowed in exceptional circumstances with proper reasoning for such deviation. The Defence cannot now say a simple decision reconsidering the Trial Chamber's strong preferences and not absolute rules violates their rights and justifies such a significant adjournment of these proceedings. Moreover, the Defence does not show a significant impact on its preparations in the motion. Even if the Chamber does not deem this argument waived, the Chamber -- Defence attempts to explain why its preparations have been impeded by the decision in paragraph 9 of the motion, where it raises five arguments. First, the Defence complains that the decision permits the Prosecution to tender multiple witness statements if the second statement is supplementary or on a distinct subject. Second, the Defence criticises the Chamber's decision to adopt a flexible approach to the presentation of exhibits through 92 bis and 92 ter witnesses. Third, the Prosecution's time-limits for Rule 92 ter witnesses have been increased according to the Defence, while the Defence has not been given additional time for cross-examination. Fourth, the Defence challenges the Chamber's decision to permit the use of transcript evidence in certain instances. Finally, the Defence complains that under the decision the Prosecution has the option of introducing documents in re-direct examination. These arguments mis-characterise the Chamber's decision, the guide-lines, and the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. The decision is fully consistent with the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. Regarding the Defence's ability to prepare in general, and particularly relevant to the first two Defence assertions, the Prosecution has not altered its Rule 92 ter package for any witness on the basis of this decision. The Defence has known what the Prosecution would seek to tender for each of the witnesses who will testify in the next two witnesses, and in most cases for a month or more. This afforded the Defence ample time to prepare. The Defence also mis-characterises the decisions -- discussion of time for examination of witnesses. The Chamber had already accepted the Prosecution's estimated examination lengths on the 24th of April, 2012, at page 314 of the transcript. While cross-examination time was not clearly at issue in the decision, the Chamber has been clear in, for instance, paragraph 11 of its decision regarding Witness Harland and paragraph 13 regarding Witnesses Kingori, Koster, and Schmitz that time for cross-examination will be evaluated after a witness has given evidence in chief on the basis of that evidence. The Defence argument regarding transcript evidence is also misleading. The decision explains certain circumstances under which transcript evidence may be admissible. As the Defence recognised in its 16th of April filing, the guide-lines always permitted deviation such as the admission of transcript evidence. Finally, the Defence asserts that the decision changes the guide-lines by permitting the Prosecution to introduce exhibits during re-examination. This is incorrect. The decision simply recognises that parties may admit exhibits during cross-examination; and if the cross-examining party opens the door to discussion of an exhibit, the party calling the witness may also introduce exhibits during re-examination. The guide-lines had not -- have not spoken to this issue which is basic to an adversarial examination. Your Honour, that completes the Prosecution's response to this motion. Your Honour, I see the time is two minutes before the break. Although my submissions on the other motions are much briefer, I will be led by the Court whether it wishes me to do that before or after the break.

To ask the Prosecution to respond in the abstract or to decide such an issue in the abstract is unnecessary and it is not explicitly authorised by any Rule in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Those future statements formatted in compliance with the guidance which it does intend to tender should be given to the Defence as soon as they are completed." The Prosecution is in full compliance with that guidance. The other two documents, Your Honour, are a map book or what we refer to as a map book with some useful maps and photographs of the Sarajevo area and the second document is simply a photograph, a satellite photograph, of the Greater Sarajevo area with neighbourhoods marked and the confrontation lines marked. If it facilitates matters today, the Prosecution is willing to simply ask foundational questions from Mr. Harland about his examination of those documents, but not seek to tender them today but simply leave them marked as 65 ter numbers until such time as the matter can be fully explored or fully discussed. Those are my submissions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: David Harland served as a civil affairs officer and political advisor to the commander of the United Nations Protection Force, or UNPROFOR, in Bosnia and Herzegovina from June 1993 until the end of the conflict. He remained in Sarajevo working for the United Nations until 1999. Mr. Harland arrived in Sarajevo approximately one year after the outbreak of hostilities and frequently attended meetings with leaders from all sides of the conflict, including both Karadzic and Mladic. He participated in negotiations concerning, among other things, freedom of movement for civilians and UNPROFOR and restoration of essential services to Sarajevo. He was the principal drafter of political reports and authored many weekly and special reports. The UN Secretary-General also tasked him with writing a report regarding events in Srebrenica during the summer of 1995, a report he filed in 1997. Mr. Harland's evidence in substantial part concerns events in Sarajevo. He provides evidence that a large number of shells were fired into Sarajevo most days, with significant lulls during the 1994 cease-fire. Such shelling was dispersed randomly across the densely populated city and had no discernible military purpose. The flow of food and utilities, including water, electricity, and gas, was largely controlled by the Bosnian Serb side and was wholly inadequate and sometimes interrupted by intentional actions of one or both sides. Mr. Harland met Mr. Mladic approximately 20 times between 1993 and 1995. Mr. Harland describes his observations of Mr. Mladic and the observations he made which led him to see Mladic as a commander with complete command and control over his military subordinates. Your Honour, that is the end of the summary. And I do see that the technical problem, I believe, has been overcome and Mr. Harland seems to be indicating that he can see it now before him.

A version of this map is contained in the map book at page 2. Before I ask the witness any questions about the exhibit, I would note that the Trial Chamber has taken extensive judicial notice of previously adjudicated facts regarding the confrontation lines around Sarajevo. These are facts 1919 to 1922, 1948 to 49, 1954 to 59, 1961 to 64, 1966 to 67, 1975, 1986, and 2020 to 2021. The Prosecution will not adduce evidence from Mr. Harland about specifics of his knowledge about the confrontation line and relies on this map simply to give the Chamber an overall graphic representation and approximation of those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, in preparation for your testimony here today, did I ask you to review several maps?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is the map that we now see on the screen before us, 28319, one of the maps you were asked to review?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What is depicted in the map?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: The urban area of Sarajevo and its environs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And according to your knowledge and your work in Sarajevo, what does the red lines represent?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: The red lines represent the forward position of Serb forces at a particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the blue lines?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Represent the forward positions of the Bosnian army at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 30 of your statement sets out your basis for familiarity. At this scale these lines can only be an approximation. In your view are they an accurate approximation of the confrontation lines around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The map has the name of a number of locations set out in yellow. My question to you is whether these place names fairly represent the approximate location of these places?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: They do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, talking about the red and the blue lines, could you please re-read the answers and look at the map again and then consider whether there's any risk of confusion. I see around the urban area first red lines. We haven't heard evidence on that yet, but I do understand from the indictment that it's the Prosecution's case that the Serbs were around Sarajevo and that the Presidency troops were inside Sarajevo. I see first the red lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I haven't been clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm looking at ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the screen there is a map which looks very much like number 2 on the -- page 2 on our binder but apparently is not -- no, the colours are just the opposite from what we find on page 2, isn't it, apart from all the names added to the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. I do recognise that that could be a source of confusion, and I think probably it's not wise to have the two versions of the map in use. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And especially not if you have changed blue by red and red by blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Particularly confusing, Your Honour. The Prosecution will be relying on the map that's on the screen in e-court and I will have the map in the map book corrected and a replacement made as soon as I am able.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- we'll then wait for the final map because the one on the screen is not -- but we'll manage. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe I had tendered this exhibit. I don't know if Mr. Lukic -- it seems to be somewhat related to his motion of yesterday. I'm not sure whether he still opposes the map, now having seen it and heard the evidence that I'm leading about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we answer this question after this gentleman finishes his examination because for now we don't know what's -- what is on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I can imagine that -- I don't know whether you have a hard copy of it or not. And I do understand that it depicts 1995 confrontation lines, suggesting that they were during the whole of that year the same. Mr. Groome, is that how I have to understand? Or perhaps the witness could --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, could I ask you to briefly discuss the confrontation lines and how much did they vary over the course of your time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: They varied rather little over the period that I was there from the spring of 1993 until the end of the war at the of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the general shape of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but for 1995 there were slight differences over the period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There would be small --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Small differences were made when an offensive by the Bosnian army might take a small amount of territory, but insignificant at this scale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would also note that in paragraph 30 of the statement Mr. Harland refers to another confrontation line map. This is a map created by the Army of the Republika Srpska and is identified as ERN 05059848 in the statement. I note for the Chamber that this is in page 56 and 57 of the map book before you. Your Honours, could I ask that 65 ter 28316 be brought to the screen. This is electronic version of the map book before you. The particular -- and I ask that we go to e-court page 65. This particular page, Your Honours, is a more detailed map of the confrontation lines which will assist the Chamber as we adduce evidence related to Sarajevo. The initial overview map is followed by a series of maps which are in large versions of the first map divided into 16 equally sized sections. They are available in e-court as pages 65 to 81 and are in the map book at pages 58 to 74 -- yes, 58 to 74.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, in preparation for your testimony, did I ask you to look at this series of maps consisting of an overview map and a series of 16 enlargements of that map?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Prior to coming to court, did I show you this series of maps on the e-court system?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, review these maps?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did I ask you to pay particular attention to the lines drawn on the map and ask that if you were able to verify that these accurately represented the confrontation lines around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you study these lines; and if so, do they, in your view, accurately represent the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: I did and they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would ask that 65 ter 28316, the Sarajevo map book, be marked for identification. The book will be used for a number of witnesses over the course of the Prosecution case and the foundation for its contents will be established with a number of witnesses. The Prosecution will tender the exhibit once the foundation for all of its contents have been established or upon the Defence indicating it does not oppose its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Groome, when you were talking about the map book, would that be what you provided to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would be the map and the photograph book.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, in electronic form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then it's clear. And I take it once you intend to replace page 2 by a map with better colours that you'll address the Chamber so that we could give permission to Madam Registrar to change that one page of the book. Madam Registrar, the number for this book to be marked for identification would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28316 becomes Exhibit P3, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. You may proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, in your view, did the topography of Sarajevo have an impact on what happened there between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please explain.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: The urban area of Sarajevo lies in a long, steep valley, as is evident on the maps. And in general the civilian population of this city and the Bosnian army defenders of the city were in the densely packed floor of the valley. And, in general, the besieging Serb forces controlled the surrounding high ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we please go to paragraph 276 of P1, Mr. Harland's statement. It can be found on page 83 of the original English and page 59 of the B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, the first two sentences of paragraph 276 of your statement read: "The Serbs frequently made the assertion that before the war broke out 65 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina was owned by the Bosnian Serbs according to, for example, title deeds. My own office did some research on the matter and we disagreed with that finding." Can I ask you to elaborate on the research that your office did into this claim and any of your office's findings that you can recall.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we had access to some of the land records in Sarajevo. We also hired in our office a professional statistician in order to deal with the claims that were made of fact by one side or the other, which were often at variance with the truth. And in particular, on this issue Professor Koljevic, one of the vice-presidents of Republika Srpska, was fond of asserting that 65 per cent of the land of Bosnia and Herzegovina was Serb and that this was the amount of territory that the Serbs should be given. And when we looked into it, it appeared that large amounts of state-owned land, including largely uninhabited territories, were attributed to the Serbs in the maps and the documents and the statements from the Pale authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you attempt to verify these claims?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND
utterances.text: Yes, we did. The land records did not confirm that the Serbs control or owned 65 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the contrary, large amounts of the territory was state-owned territory and sparsely or uninhabited.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, could I ask one clarifying question. You started by saying that you had access to some of the land records. Later you referred to the land records. Were you referring to the "some" you had had access to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you further explain what those "some" were, apparently not covering all of the land records.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. The full original cadastral records were not available to my office. Some of the original records were available, and for the rest of the territory we had secondary data, such as the 1990 census results. But we did not have the full records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do the census results indicate any ownership of land, apart from who was populating it? Does it refer to ownership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It refers to your place of residence and your -- the ethnicity that you had identified for yourself, and it was a choice of several ethnicities you could choose, Muslim, Serb, Croat, Yugoslav, and other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How could they then assist you in defining who owned what property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The assertion made by Professor Koljevic and the Serb authorities was really by way of saying 65 per cent of Bosnia is ours. Either we own it or we live on it or it's historically ours. And when we looked into those aspects of it that we could look into, it was not confirmed by the records that came to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, you are rather criticising the method used by Mr. Koljevic than that you answered my question, isn't it? My question was: How could they, being the census results, then assist you into finding who owned what property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, they did not establish ownership at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then my question remains: How could they then assist you in assessing who owned what property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at all, except that they show who lives where. The actual legal status of the piece of land you are on, whether it's private property or social property or state property, which I think are the three legal categories that they had in their pre-war system, were not indicated in the 1991 census. You are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the census results would not in any way assist you in defining who is the owner of what percentage of the land?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you said you had secondary data such as the 1990 census results, which would fill in the gap which was there because you did not have all of the cadastral records, but they therefore could not fill in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When, for example, there is large uninhabited territories which on the maps we were given in Pale were indicated as Serb and which were known to be not shown by the census data not to be inhabited, then we assumed that it was not correct to ascribe them to one community or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You now in your answer use for the first time the word "we assumed." Would you agree with me that part of your verification was based on assumptions rather than on facts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
